source.title: The Implicit Bias of Gradient Descent on Separable Data
source.authors: Daniel Soudry; Elad Hoffer; Suriya Gunasekar; N. Srebro

record.file_problem: The supplied text contains the full paper.
record.tranche_reason: The paper reports a conceptual test of continued generalization after training error reaches zero, using a convolutional-network training curve on CIFAR10. It does not test the versions’ specified interventions or measures.
record.gate_note: The CIFAR10 experiment reports training and validation errors at six epochs; these results do not test random-label memorization or any version’s specified mechanism. The optimizer figures compare convergence directions on a toy separable dataset, not held-out generalization. Optimizer-generalization comparisons in the text are cited prior work.
record.test_reason: The study's own results concern implicit max-margin bias and continued training at fixed architecture. None tests V1–V8: the CIFAR-10 trajectory varies epochs rather than width, and the Adam comparison measures separator direction rather than held-out performance. Generalization comparisons relevant to the versions are cited prior work.
record.authors_conclusion: The record accurately paraphrases the CIFAR-10 example but omits the main conclusion: under stated assumptions, gradient descent on separable homogeneous linear prediction converges in direction to the L2 max-margin solution, much more slowly than training loss converges. The authors argue that validation classification error can remain useful for monitoring training even when validation loss rises; the deep-network theory covers restricted settings.
record.recipe_differences: The CIFAR10 experiment is a neural-network training trajectory, not the random-label experiments or controlled comparisons in the claim versions. Theoretical analysis focuses on homogeneous linear predictors and a restricted single-layer setting.
record.method_sensitivity: Training epoch changes the reported train and validation errors; validation error is not monotonic across the sampled epochs.

fits_no_version.finding: At epochs 2000 and 4000, reported training error remains zero while validation error changes from 8.92% to 8.9%; validation loss rises from 1.01 to 1.18.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Continued optimization at fixed architecture can improve validation classification error after zero training error, even while validation cross-entropy increases.

fits_no_version.finding: Theorems 3 and 5 establish slow directional convergence of gradient descent to the L2 max-margin separator for separable homogeneous linear prediction with suitable exponential-tail losses.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Gradient descent has an implicit max-margin bias under the stated separability, loss, and step-size assumptions.

fits_no_version.finding: Figure 3 reports that Adam and gradient descent both reach zero training error on synthetic separable data, but Adam does not approach the L2 max-margin direction.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Optimization algorithms can select different separating directions despite both fitting the training labels.

record.problems: The deep-network generalization evidence is one CIFAR10 convolutional-network example; architecture size and sample counts are not stated. The paper calls the validation-error change slow, but reports no uncertainty estimates for the table values.
record.rows_left_out: No results were left out under the 60-row limit. The toy separable-data optimizer figures and cited comparisons do not report the held-out generalization outcomes named in the claim versions.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and natural-versus-random held-out performance under the same architecture and recipe.
Width sweeps and test error beyond the width needed for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected generalization and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive-versus-SGD held-out performance under limited or broader tuning and recovery interventions.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and recipe adaptations.
Dropout effects, training-set-size dependence, underfitting, and removal with weight decay.
Magnitude-aware sharpness, its correlation with generalization gaps, and ranking against other measures.
Retraining after removal of highly memorized versus random examples.

record.verdict_notes: All twelve numerical values match Table 1. The 0.02-percentage-point late validation-error improvement has no reported uncertainty. Figure 2's caption separately reports 8.3% final validation error, without specifying its epoch; this does not replace Table 1's 4000-epoch value of 8.9%.

versions.untested_parts: Does not train on random labels or compare natural-label and random-label training with the same architecture and recipe.
No width sweep or interpolation-threshold comparison.
No comparison of convolutional and fully connected architectures.
Does not compare held-out performance of adaptive optimizers and SGD on image or language benchmarks. The adaptive-optimizer result shown compares separator directions on a toy dataset.
No magnitude-aware sharpness measurement or comparison with norm- and margin-based generalization measures.
